The speaker wonders about the power the thawing ground swells show each spring, which is later contrasted with the destruction wrought by careless hunters. The last section focuses on the relationship between the speaker and his neighbor, both New England farmers, and characterizes their spring activity as an "outdoor game." For 10 points--, identify this forty-five line blank verse poem that ends with the line "Good fences make good neighbors."

In the first chapter of this work, the author recalls letters exchanged in 1797 between Goethe and Schiller on the "retarding element" in Homeric literature. The last chapter focuses on Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse and is often published independently under the title The Brown Stocking. Throughout the work the author seeks to trace the development of realism in literature and claims that modern realism was born in the character Julien Sorel. Named for the concept which Aristotle contrasted to diegesis --for 10 points-- name this history of representation in literature by Erich Auerbach.

This play is resolved after the character Jasper feigns death, impersonates his own ghost, scares his master, and wins the hand of his master's daughter Luce. The play was a burlesque of Heywood's Four Prentices of London and begins with a grocer and his wife entering the theater to see The London Merchant and insisting their boy Ralph (Rafe) have a part in the production. For 10 points-- name this drama by Beaumont and Fletcher named for the object depicted on Ralph's shield.

The first story in this collection, "Children of the Sea," examines a pair of lovers separated by the tyranny of their country's government through love letters. A girl named Lamort helps an American journalist find her missing mother in "The Missing Peace," but they are almost shot when they witness soldiers dragging a dead body into a graveyard. The last story is "Caroline's Wedding" features a mother in America trying to deal with her daughter marrying a Bahamian outside of the church. Comprised of 9 stories in all, For 10 points-- name this collection by Edwidge Danticat, which takes its name from the typical greeting that precedes stories told by native Haitians.

Pinhas, one of the characters created by this man, is described as having "One small eye and one big eye." His autobiography, subtitled "Scenes from my childhood" is entitled The Great Fair. Other characters in his broad repertoire include Menahem-Mendl and the Cantor's son, Mottel, the latter of whom was recreated as a tailor in a compilation of this man's work centered around another of his characters, a dairyman named Tevye. For 10 points-- name this paragon of Yiddish literature whose tales were adapted into the musical Fiddler on the Roof.

In the first chapter of this novel, the protagonists are harassed by a comb-seller on a train to an unnamed coastal city. The train is stopped after several people are found on the tracks attempting suicide in response to the national emergency. Ishvar Doji and his nephew Omprakash flee their lower- caste origins and join the naïve college student Maneck Kolah in boarding with the widowed seamstress Dina Dalal. For 10 points-- name this novel by Rohinton Mistry about the aftermath of a state of emergency called by Indira Gandhi.

Five years after using an American teaching stint as the basis for the novel One Fat Englishman, this author used the pseudonym Robert Markham for his novel Colonel Sun. A story about the arrival of Alun and Rhinannon Weaver and its effect on Malcolm, Peter and Charlie is explored in the Booker Prize winning Old Devils. Sometimes associated poetically with the angry young men --for 10 points-- name this English author, whose most famous protagonist is Jim Dixon.

A collection entitled "Journey into a dustless realm" was released to honor the seventieth birthday of this poet, who once claimed to "represent the tragedy of the Jewish people." Drawing from the tradition of mystic Jakob Böhme, Nobel laureate Selma Lagerlöf was her frequent correspondent and assisted her escape from Nazi Germany. The author of works such as "O the Chimneys" and "In the habitations of Death" \--for 10 points-- name this German author who shared the Nobel Prize in 1966 with Yosef Agnon.

The song "My True love hath my heart" was included with this 1580 prose work whose author began it as an amusement for his sister, the countess of Pembroke. The plot begins when Musidorus and Pyrocles are shipwrecked. In the drama Philastor, Beaumont and Fletcher based the character Bellario on Zelmane, the woman whom Pyrocles disguises himself as in order to win the hand of Philoclea. Finally resolved after the death and resurrection of the father of Philoclea and king of the namesake pastoral region --for 10 points-- name this 17th century prose romance by Philip Sidney.

"Shall I strew on thee rose or rue or laurel," opens a poem of this title dedicated to the memory of French poet. Another work uses this title and requests "Row us out from Desenzano, to your Sirmione row!" Both works draw on a first century B.C. Poet who in his 101st poem mourns the loss of a brother. Used in the titles of works by Swinburne and Tennyson --for 10 points—give this Latin phrase which was first used by Catullus and which is often translated "Hail and Farewell."

Franklin Pierce Adams wrote a take off of this poem parodying Freud. The line "Not enjoyment, and not sorrow, is our destined end or way," indicates the poet's disbelief in Epicureanism, while "Life is real - life is earnest - and the grave in not its goal" indicates a belief in eternal life. First published in Knickerbocker Magazine, it later appeared in the poet's first published collection, Voices in the Night and its subtitle indicates that it describes "What the heart of the young man says" to the author. For 10 points--, identify this poem which includes the "Art is long, and Time is fleeting," by Longfellow.

In 1728 Lewis Theobald published a drama called Double Falsehood, which he claimed was a "revised and adapted" version of this play. In 2004 Oxford's Burton Taylor Theatre claimed to be producing the first production of this work since its recovery by Charles Hamilton from a manuscript previously attributed to Middleton known as the Second Maiden's Tragedy. Named for the lover of Lucinda in Don Quixote \--for 10 points-- name this infamous play by Fletcher and Shakespeare which may or may not be extant.

In one of the stories in this collection Dick feels what he calls the Omne Animal after having sex with Lois in a barn. A girl gets a glimpse into her father's past when they make a sales call to one of his old sweethearts in "Walker Brothers Cowboy." The title story of the collection concerns a piano recital whose unexpected star is a mildly retarded girl who plays the title piece of music to the joy of those around her. For 10 points-- name this collection of short stories set in western Ontario by Alice Munro.

In the American Grain is a collection of his essays, while Spring and All is a collection of mixed poetry and prose. His marriage was the subject of "Asphodel, that Greeny Flower" while his short stories are published in The Edge of the Knife and Life Along the Passaic River. He invented the "triadic" or "stepped line" while working on his most famous work, and wrote the poetry collections including The Desert Music and Pictures from Brueghel, For 10 points-- name this poet of Paterson.

After the first performance of this drama, its author circulated the Excuse to Ariste in response to criticism. The central quarrel of the play is begun by an argument over the tutelage of the King's son, but in the span of a day eventually leads to the title character fighting two duels, one against Don Sanche and one against Don Gomes, respectively the suitor and father of his beloved, Chimene, and leading a nighttime raid against the moors that earns him the titular distinction. FTP name this 1636 play about Don Rodrigue, the most famous work of Pierre Corneille.

The most infamous line in this drama occurred after the widow Quin asks for some starch and Margaret replies, "And you without a white shift or a shirt in your whole family since the drying of the flood. I've no starch for the like of you." Margaret is the play's protagonist's second cousin and he wins her hand in marriage in a mule race after his arrival in Mayo. Centering on the patricidal Christy Mahon whose nickname gives the play its title --for 10 points-- name this J.M. Synge drama whose reference to a women's undergarment caused a riot.

In a public display of charity, Mrs. Poulteney takes in the title character of this novel that is set near Wessex in Lyme Regis. During a walk with his fiancé Ernestina, the protagonist, who is a baronet's nephew and an amateur paleontologist, meets the title character and becomes infatuated with her. After she vanishes, the protagonist searches for her for twenty months and when he finds her, the author offers multiple conclusions to the novel. Sarah Woodruff is --for 10 points-- what titular female in a 1967 pseudo- Victorian novel by John Fowles?

One side plot of this novel concerns Gaffer's daughter's courtship by two suitors. An heir, who is being blackmailed by the taxidermist Venus and peddler Wegg, hires the lawyer Mortimer Lightwood to investigate the death of his employee and benefactor. Eventually Lightwood and his client Boffin learn that the mysterious Rokesmith, who is romantically involved with Bella Wilfer, is actually Hanford and that the central character is not really dead. For 10 points-- name this last of Dickens' completed novels, whose title character is John Harmon.

The title character drops his copy of Caesar's Commentaries and considers himself only a blunt soldier. He enlists his friend John's help, but this results in John contemplating returning to England and the title character returning from the warpath with a savage's head. John finally marries after the title character is rumored dead from a poisoned error. For 10 points--, identify this poem where Pricilla rejects a proposal, a work by Longfellow.

In the first scene of this play, a slave tells another about a dream in which a whale is yelling at some sheep dressed in cloaks. Those slaves, Sosias and Xanthus, assist in a ruse in which two men dressed as dogs argue over the theft of some Sicilian cheese in front of the title characters, who act as the jury. The basis for Racine's only comedy, The Litigants, --for 10 points—name this Aristophanes work satirizing the Athenian justice system.

In the 107th line of this poem, the lead male character sings the song "Tirra lirra, tirra lirra." That character stands amongst "fields of barley and of rye / That clothe the wold and meet the sky" on the bank of the river lie. The author claimed that basis of the poem was the Italian tale which centered on a fair maid who wove portraits based on a mirror's reflection. Originally published in 1832 and greatly altered ten years later, --for 10 points-- name this poem in which the story of Launcelot and Elaine is told by Tennyson.

He was a member of "Kelly's Army" which crossed the country but failed to join Coxey's Army. His involvement with the socialist movement is seen in works like The People of the Abyss and The Law of Life. His autobiographical Martin Eden is not as well known as the collection Tales of the Far North, which includes stories like "The Son of the Wolf" and "To Build a Fire." For 10 points-- name this American author known for novels like Sea Wolf and Call of the Wild.

Chapters in this novel feature the title character "In the Dismal Swamp," "On a Field Trip" and "In the Country." The protagonist twists the arm of George Bramhall in a wine cellar, and muses that he is twisting the arms of Desperate, Broken-hearted and Disillusioned-with-tubercular-husband. When the protagonist falls ill he is told he should live in the South Seas and marry a girl "in whose eyes is an ancient wisdom" by his boss, Shrike, while a trip to the country is suggested by his girlfriend Betty. FTP name this novel about a disillusioned advice columnist by Nathaniel West.

His wife tries to convince him to see Dr. Renshaw while in town for errands and the Waterbury trial, a trip to the A&P, and Liberty Magazine all prompt his fantasies. He almost hits a Buick wile dreaming about being a world-famous surgeon who repairs an anesthetizer on the fly with a fountain pen. A timid middle-aged man dominated by his wife, he imagines himself as a pilot, soldier, and other glamorous occupations. FTP, identify this man whose secret life was written about by James Thurber.

Edith Sitwell's choice of inclusions for the anthology Wheels was chosen to oppose the "idyllic quietism" of this group. Edward Marsh edited the group's second anthology that included "Seven Seals" by D.H. Lawrence and numerous selections from the War Poems of Siegfried Sassoon. Including poets Edmund Blunden, Walter de la Mare, and Rupert Brooke --for 10 points-- name this group of twentieth century British poets that took its name from a British King.

Albrecht Dürer wrote in his diary that he owned a copy of the most famous book about him, the author of which, known only as "N", is thought to be Hermann Bote. According to the book he was born around 1300 in Kneitlingen and baptized thrice, once at the altar, once in a muddy river and again in a warm bath. The Latin phrase Hic Fuit is said to have accompanied his namesake sign of an owl and a mirror whenever this character made mischief in an area in which he was not well known. For 10 points-- name this ubiquitous jester of German myth.

This author, who titled his memoir Flaws in the Glass, failed in an attempt to dramatize Henry James' Aspern Papers. He was contemptuous of his parent's social ambitions and like his character Hurtle Duffield in The Vivisector rebelled against the class to which he was born. In his best-known work, which won the inaugural Miles Franklin Award, the German title character attempts to cross the desert of the continent's interior. For 10 points-- name this Australian Nobel laureate and writer of The Aunt's Story and Voss.

Her work "The Will of Change" takes it title from the opening line of Charles Olson's The Kingfishers while her second book, The Diamond Cutters was published shortly after her marriage to economist Alfred Conrad. Her opposition to the Vietnam War is reflected in the poems in Leaflets, including "Orion" and "Implosions," while her long poem "Sources" explores her relationships with her Jewish husband and father. For 10 points-- name this modern American female poet of "Diving into the Wreck."

During a stint living in America, this author met Upton Sinclair and was convinced by him into becoming a Socialist. Later in life, he repudiated his former views in the 1963 essay collection, A Writer's Schooling. In his novel Paradise Reclaimed, he presents a satiric portrayal of the Mormons in his native land. His dramatic works include The Chimney Play and The Pigeon Banquet, while his novels You Pure Vine and The Bird on the Shore comprise his Salka Valka and concern life in a fishing village. Best known for a trilogy comprised of Fire in Copenhagen, The Slender Fairy, and Iceland's Ball, this is, what Icelandic winner of the 1955 Nobel Prize in Literature?

The finale of the poem contains an allusion to the story of Venus and Adonis, particularly the white anemone that springs from the end of their affair. One of the poems contains an epigraph from Seneca'a Medea. The epigram from the first poem is a quote from the Book of Job, and is spoken by Satan. Section Three contains snatches of conversation overheard at waterfront bars interspersed with visions of undersea mythological creatures and is titled "Cutty Sark." Other sections include, "National Winter Garden," "Van Winkle" and "Cape Hatteras." identify this long poem about a New York landmark, the masterwork of Hart Crane.

He shares his name with a jealous acquaintance of Bellerophon who sends the hero on a journey to deliver his own death warrant to King Iobates of Lycia. Various sources place his home on the island of Carpathus between Crete and Rhodes. His most famous visitor approached him on the advice of his own daughter, Eidothea. Stranded on the Egyptian island of Pharos, Menelaus, dressed as a seal, accosted him during a midday nap, and subdued him as he changed into a lion, a dragon, a leopard, a boar, a film of water, and a tree. Name this reluctant old prophet who, through his metamorphoses, has become a symbol for primeval matter.

The play starts with a discussion of the recent murder of Robbie Tancred. The discussion is interrupted by the entrance of Jerry Devine, who comes with a job offer from Father Farrell. The job is not taken, and two days later the family is visited by Charlie Bentham, who announces that a cousin had bequeathed the family 2,000 pounds. In the end, Johnny is killed for his supposed part in Tancred's murder. After this, the title character and her daughter leave, and Captain Jack and his friend Joxer return to the house drunk. The Boyle family are at the center of, what drama named for a goddess and her favorite pet and written by Sean O'Casey?

The poem of which he is the subject is the sole surviving example of the Heldenlieder in Old High German, although a later ballad provides a sequel involving a reconciliation. The original, though incomplete, leaves little doubt that the duel ends fatally for his brash son, who instigates the challenge without knowing that his opponent is also his father. The elder warrior was also a magician and served as weapons adviser to Dietrich von Bern, the legendary version of Theodoric the Great. Name this hero who also appears in the Nibelungenlied, where as a member of Etzel's court, he slays Kriemhild for ordering the slaughter of her brothers, and who shares his name with Pope Gregory VII.

Charles Townshend was so taken with this book that he hired its author to tutor his stepson, the Duke of Buccleuch [pron. Buckley]. Part Seven contains an illuminating explication of Stoicism. Part Five includes a discussion of the importance of fashion and custom on shaping human notions of beauty. The second part discusses how luck influences the foundations of human value judgments, while the third part discusses the foundations of conscience. The book opens with a discussion of sympathy and the propriety of an action. Identify this work which examines the origins of our standards of right and wrong, a work by Adam Smith.

In 1840, he wrote a witty book about Ludwig Borne, the leader of the German radicals in Paris, which earned him the ire of many socialists. Politically involved, he wrote for Karl Marx's newspaper Forward, and authored a satire in verse, Germany, A Winter's Tale. His criticism of German Romanticism was published in France as Lutezia, and in Germany as The Romantic School. His New Poems is divided into the "New Spring" poems, which are love poems, and "Varia", sour poems about his dalliances with Paris girls. Other poems include "Atta Troll" and "Romanzero," though his first collection, Buch der Leider, is more famous. Identify this German-Jewish poet, author of "Die Lorelei."

He published some of his short fiction in The Overland Monthly and The Atlantic Monthly, including "The Passing of Cockeye Blacklock," and "Comida: An Experience in Famine." His devotion to truthful fiction is expounded in his famous essay "The Responsibilities of a Novelist." His adventure novels include A Man's Woman, which dealt with Arctic exploration, Blix, which was published posthumously, and Moran of the Lady Letty. One of his novels was made into a film by Erich von Stroheim under the title Greed, and concerns a demented dentist. Identify this American naturalist, the author of McTeague and The Epic of the Wheat.

He wrote The War with the Newts, a 1936 novel that satirizes the rise of totalitarianism in the form of a race of intelligent salamanders that take over Europe. He collaborated with his brother Josef on a number of works, including the short story collection The Luminous Depths, and the play The Life of Insects. He also wrote a science fiction trilogy consisting of the novels Hordubal, Meteor, and An Ordinary Life. Leos Janacek based an opera on The Makropoulos Case, written by, what author of R.U.R., in which he coined the term "robot."

Legend has it that Arthur Miller turned down the chance to write the screenplay because of lingering doubts about the director and his relation to the Hollywood blacklist. The movie deals with the pressure to name names before the authorities, and some critics felt that the director had used it to justify his own collaboration with the House Un-American Activities Committee. Name the 1954 Elia Kazan movie that starred Marlon Brando, whose character responds to charges of ratting by protesting, "I was rattin' on myself all those years. I didn't even know it," and more famously explains to his brother how he "coulda been a contender."

In this play, a janitor predicts the coming murder of the milk-company collector, Sankey. A manager at the real estate office, Harry Easter, tries to set up the main character in an apartment outside the tenement, but she refuses. Abe spends his days and nights reading the newspaper and arguing politics. His daughter, Shirley, worries about her brother Sam Kaplan's interest in the heroine, who just wants to leave the city. In the end, Frank catches his wife Anna in bed with Sankey, and kills them both, enabling Rose, their daughter and heroine, to get out of the slums. Identify this play about the Maurrant family, the most famous of Elmer Rice.

A recently refuted legend says this novel was written in a week to finance the funeral of the author's mother. It features a Stoic philosopher who preaches the life of reason, but his view is undermined by the death of his daughter and his subsequent grief. After staying in a monastery after being kidnapped, Pekuah decides that the life of a nun is the surest way to happiness. The poet Imlac wants to live a life of wandering, while Nekayah, the title character's sister, desires to found a women's college. The title character merely wants to rule a kingdom justly. Identify this satiric novel about the prince of Abyssinia, written by Samuel Johnson.

The character of William M. Weed is obviously based upon the real-life Boss Tweed. Senator Dilworthy attempts to get an appropriation bill passed in Congress that will turn a farm into a freedmen's university. The adopted daughter of Squire "Si" Hawkins, goes to Washington to try to get the bill passed, but is forced to kill a would-be suitor, Colonel Shelby. In the end, Laura is acquitted of all crimes. A sequel to it was written with William Dean Howells as a play and later a novel, titled The American Claimant. Name this novel in which Charles Warner and Mark Twain created the character of Colonel Beriah Sellers.

Because of a reference in his poem, "Tears to Thamysis", it is known that he was educated at Westminster. In 1627 he was a chaplain to the unlucky expedition to the Isle of Rhe. He died unmarried, but wrote erotic poetry to a woman named Julia. Swinburne called him England's greatest song-writer, and the 17th-century English composer Henry Lawes set some of his songs to music. His religious poetry was collected in "His Noble Numbers," which is contained in a larger collection, Hesperides. Identify this Cavalier poet of "To Daffodils", "The Vine", and "To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time."

After receiving a grant from the MacArthur Foundation in 1981, she began her second novel, which took ten years to write. Meanwhile, she released the collection Storyteller and The Delicacy and Strength of Lace, a selection of her correspondence with poet James Wright. Her The Almanac of the Dead spans 500 years and focuses on a Tucson family traveling to Africa and Israel. Her first novel featured World War II veteran Tayo learning that the noun of the title referred to not just formal ritual but also a lifestyle. Name this Native American author who penned Ceremony.

In Thomas Mann's The Magic Mountain, he is portrayed as Naphta, a Jewish- born Jesuit in dire need of authority. His work The Historical Novel is primarily a study of the innovations of Sir Walter Scott. He stressed the distinction between actual class consciousness and ascribed class consciousness, that is, what the proletariat would have done if it knew all the facts. In works such as Old and New Culture and Studies in European Realism, he attacked literary formalism and drew a link between art and social struggle. His most famous work, History and Class Consciousness: Studies In Marxist Dialectics, was criticized by hard-line Marxists. Identify this Hungarian-born Marxist critic.

He forced a rival, Pietro Gratarol, from Venice by the authorship of a mocking satirical play, The Drugs of Love. After the success of a satirical poem, "La tartana degl'influssi", he began work on his ten Fiabe or fables, including "The King Stag," "The Snake Woman," and "The Pretty Little Green Bird." Attacking the dramatic innovations of Carlo Goldoni and Pietro Chiari, he joined the reactionary Accademia dei Granelleschi [gra-nel-ESS-kee] and depicted them in a famous play as a magician and a wicked fairy identify this great Italian dramatist, most famous for The Love of the Three Oranges and Turandot.

While working as a pathologist at Bellevue Hospital in New York, he contracted tuberculosis, and while recovering, decided to become a writer. In his most famous novel, he introduced the concept of "Malaise," despair inherent in the modern world. He also wrote a major work in Catholic philosophy and semantics titled The Message in the Bottle. His other works include Lancelot, The Second Coming, and Love in the Ruins, the last of which became the prequel for The Thanatos Syndrome. Identify this writer of The Moviegoer.

The title character is almost executed by a group of priests until a widow Almona saves him by offering to sleep with the priests if they pardon him. He finds a comptroller for King Nabussan of Serendib by having a dancing contest with a pile of money available to steal. The honest man dances lightly, not trying to prevent the sound of change. The hero is briefly married to Azora, whom he also tricks through the advances of his friend Cador. In the end, he wins his love from slavery by curing Ogul, and finally then wins Queen Astarte again in a tournament and becomes king of Babylon. Identify this satire about a youth who lives by his wits, written by Voltaire.

The subject of one of this author's novels is Sonny, an obscure schoolteacher-turned-radical and his writer son Will. Another is about the Bam and Maureen Smales, who must attempt to flee when anarchy seizes their native land. The author's last novel concerns Harold and Claudia, a couple whose lives are disrupted when their son is accused of murder and defended by a black lawyer, and is titled The House Gun. This author's first collection, the Soft Voice of the Serpent, and first novel, The Lying Days, both demonstrate her lack of sentimentality, and precise writing style. Identify this South African writer, who attacks apartheid in her novels The Conservationist and July's People.

His early work, while studying under Victor Bertin, was primarily calm, well structured landscapes including The Forum and Bridge at Nantes. Dividing his year between winter months spent on classical and historical subjects and summer months spent outside with his Barbizon friends, after achieving critical success his landscapes thereafter became imaginary creations bathed in a filmy romantic atmosphere achieved by silvery tones and soft brushstrokes as in Ville d'Avray and Memory of Mortefontaine. Name this inventor of the Souvenirs landscape and painter of The Harbor of La Rochelle and The Bridge at Narni.

A childhood friend of Jules Verne, a character based on him appears in the novel A Long Vacation. Elected to the chamber of deputies from the Loire department in 1902, he quickly gained fame by drafting a bill separating church and state. Breaking with Jaurs [zhwah-REZ] and the Socialists over his decision to cooperate with the radicals, he served as Clemenceau's education minister before becoming Premier in 1909 and led the government through the first 18 months of World War I. Name this 11-time premier of France who won a Nobel prize with Stresemann for helping to draft the Locarno Pact, not for his anti-war declaration with Kellogg.

While working at the Wenner-Gren in New York City, he wrote The Heart of Matter, a largely autobiographical work, as well as Activation of Energy. In Christianity and Evolution, he claims that when man turns his powers of synthesis towards life, that is science, and when man turns his powers towards the future, that is theology. His works when largely unpublished during his life, however, as they were suppressed by his Jesuit superiors. Working in life instead primarily as an paleontologist, he was famously involved in the excavation of Piltdown Man. Identify this man, who argued that the world was evolving toward an "Omega Point," in his Phenomenon of Man.

The heroine's father dies in a cottage near Chateau-le-Blanc, and she is ordered to burn a pile of letters, though she saves a picture of someone who will turn out to be the Marquise de Villeroi. Later, the heroine retires to a cottage in Tuscany, only to return with her maid, a servant named Ludovico, and Monsieur Du Pont, a friend of her father's. At the end it is revealed that the title locale actually belonged to Lady Laurentini, though through most of the novel it is in possession of Signor Montoni, who terrorizes the heroine and her aunt. In the end, all is well and the heroine marries Valancourt. Emily St. Aubert and a mysterious castle feature in, what novel by Ann Radcliffe?

In Decolonizing the Mind, this author bids "farewell to English" and describes language as a means of understanding oneself. One of this author's novels is a disjointed narrative telling the stories of the freedom fighter Kihika, and the love triangle between Mumbi and her suitors Gikonyo and Karanja. Attacking capitalism and corruption, the play I Will Marry When I Want got this author imprisoned for a year. Written in the style of traditional ballad singers, the novel Devil on the Cross is a meeting between the Devil and the exploiters of the poor. Identify this Kenyan author, known for his novels Weep Not, Child and Petals of Blood.

After playing semiprofessional baseball and dropping out of Vanderbilt University, later in life he was offered an honorary degree but turned it down because he felt degrees should be earned. In the 1890's he moved to Uvalde where he set up a practice and received The Uvalde Leader in lieu of fee. He was known for his legislative technique of "striking a blow for liberty" by inviting people to his office and getting them drunk so they would support his ideas. He was elected to the House in 1902 and served as vice-president for two terms before breaking with his president over the court-packing scandal. Name Texan, nicknamed "Cactus Jack, who was the first vice president for FDR.

Leo Tolstoy said of the author of this work that it was impossible to disagree with him once his ideas were carefully considered. The author's later work Social Problems is a shortened summary of this work. The spiritual strain in it is seen in the last chapter, "The Call of Liberty", where the author connects the end of destitution to the Second Coming. The dichotomy of the title concepts is referred to by its author in the first chapter title as "The Great Enigma of Our Times." identify this work concerned with the implementation of a single land tax to bring economic equality, the most important work of Henry George.

Examples of these by Giovanni da Cascia, Jacopo da Bologna, and others are found in the Squarcialupi Codex, a famous illuminated manuscript. Anticipated by the Mantuan frottola, originally the music showed a definite tendency to keep the melody in the top part though the later Franco- Flemish composers of this style made it increasing contrapuntal. Used in England by Nicholas Yonge [pron. Young] and Thomas Morley, many were written in praise of Elizabeth I. Name this type of love song for multiple-voice choir that was developed by Francesco Landini in Florence in the fourteenth century.

As a young man during World War II, this author helped smuggle Allied soldiers and Jewish scientists into Switzerland. His wife Franca Rame was kidnapped and tortured by fascists for their leftist political activism. His most famous play is a retelling of Passion stories, updated with modern political themes, and was denounced by the Catholic Church when it appeared on Italian television. The recently published Johan Padan and the Discovery of the Americas is a retelling of the story of Christopher Columbus. Some of his other plays include Adult Orgasm Escapes from the Zoo, and The Accidental Death of an Anarchist. Identify this Italian playwright, the author of the play Mistero Buffo.

This serious poem's lighter moments include when the poet prays to Juno and Morpheus and offers a sacrifice of featherbeds in exchange for sleep.. The theme of incomplete consolation draws on Boethius, while use of a chess game with Fortune is similar to a game in the Roman de la Rose. The poet finally falls asleep while reading the classical story of Halycon and Ceyx, and dreams of a Black Knight who laments the death of his lady love. Identify this elegy composed for John of Gaunt on the death of his wife Blanche of Lancaster, written by Geoffrey Chaucer.

Toward the end of the novel the protagonist is taken care of by an old woman named Tiare, who eventually introduces him to his second wife, Ata. After a major illness, he is nursed back to health by the wife of a fellow in his profession. Though she professes to hate him, she falls in love with him, eschewing her husband Dirk Stroeve in the process. Stroeve stalks his wife until he finds she has poisoned herself because painter and stockbroker Charles Strickland has only been using her as a model in, what novel by W. Somerset Maugham?
